# THEORYs with `tags` `endosymbiosis`

*Topics — What a work is about. The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Endosymbiosis and reductive evolution** — how one organism comes to live inside another and depend on it, and how that ends — reductive genome evolution by drift, deletional bias or adaptive loss (including the Black Queen dependencies of free-living microbes), complementary loss across partners, nested symbioses and symbiont splitting and replacement, endosymbiotic gene transfer, protein import and host control of transmission, organellogenesis and organelle loss, and eukaryogenesis. The ecology of a partnership is ecology (ADR-055).

| [THEORY-1048](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1048.md) | On the Black Queen Hypothesis of Morris, Lenski and Zinser, losing a costly function whose product leaks to neighbours is favoured by ordinary individual selection in large free-living microbial populations, and the loss proceeds until the remaining producers just supply the community, so that most cells come to depend on a rare few with no relatedness, cooperation or collective required | Morris, Lenski & Zinser (2012), [LIT-1568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1568.md), read in [NOTE-1212](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1212.md). A loss-of-function mutant invades when its resource saving B = (Q_A − Q_M)/Q_A exceeds its cost C, which falls as other cells' leaky activity protects it. Because protection falls as producers become rare, the loss is frequency dependent and stops short of community-wide loss. The evidence is Prochlorococcus's loss of katG and its dependence on a peroxide-removing community. The dependence it produces is one-way, from beneficiaries to helpers, and involves no collective. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1049.md) | On McCutcheon and colleagues' survey, bacterial endosymbionts lose their own cell-envelope and envelope-transport genes together below about 400 kb, and begin to lose translation genes (ribosomal proteins, tRNAs, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases) below about 200 kb, so that the smallest-genome symbionts cannot be self-sufficient and their membranes, transport and protein synthesis are presumably supplied by the host, as for organelles | McCutcheon, Garber, Spencer & Warren (2024), [LIT-1571](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1571.md), read in [NOTE-1213](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1213.md). The envelope goes first, near 400 kb, and translation starts to go below about 200 kb, the authors' "tipping point". Such symbionts have three-membrane envelopes and among the most biased proteomes in bacteria. They can only work if the host provides what they no longer encode. The host's role is inferred, not shown: the mechanisms are, in the paper's word, mysteries. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1050](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1050.md) | In Athreya, Czuppon and Gokhale's adaptive-dynamics model of an incipient endosymbiosis, mutual dependence (the product of the partners' obligacies) evolves ahead of reproductive cohesion (the product of their adhesions) early on, but only under the mapping in which each partner's free-living growth depends on its own obligacy alone while dissociation depends on both partners' adhesions; the authors' own appendix shows the bias vanishing under matched mappings and reversing under the opposite one, and their survey of real symbioses cannot test it | Athreya, Czuppon & Gokhale (2025), [LIT-1570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1570.md), read in [NOTE-1211](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1211.md). In the exponential version of the model, all four traits rise monotonically. Each partner becomes more obligate than adhesive, because a gain in adhesion is "damped by the other adhesion" in the dissociation rate. Table S1 shows this is a consequence of that mapping: matched mappings give no bias, and the opposite mapping biases trajectories towards cohesion. The record's summary of the result, "even when investments are uncorrelated", is true of the traits' genetic correlation but not of their functional coupling, which is what decides it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1051.md) | In Athreya, Czuppon and Gokhale's model of an incipient endosymbiosis, the partner with the larger and faster-growing population evolves faster and becomes fully obligate first, a Red King effect in which the collective's shared fate aligns interests; the other partner's dependence then stays where it was, rises to full dependence, or falls to none, according to whether partners are born or die inside the collective, and dependence rises at all only if the collective's carrying capacity is high enough, so a full transition to a mutually dependent, co-reproducing pair is a parameter-dependent outcome and not the default | Athreya, Czuppon & Gokhale (2025), [LIT-1570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1570.md), read in [NOTE-1211](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1211.md). With the symbiont's population larger and faster, its obligacy reaches 1 first. In the base model the host's R₀ is then exactly 1, so host obligacy is neutral. With within-collective deaths the host goes fully obligate, and with within-collective births it goes back to independence. Obligacy rises from zero only if the collective's carrying capacity exceeds about aK_HK_S/d; collective growth rate does not matter. The authors take the model as a null: a transition "is far from an inevitable outcome of the existence of a higher level of selection". | Proposed |
